extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of literary/philosophical lectures on religion and heroism
extracted.subtask_description: A 19th-century lecture-style literary/philosophical analysis comparing Norse mythology and the figure of the Prophet (Mahomet), describing qualities that define religions, heroes, and prophets. The text argues for particular moral, social, and aesthetic criteria by which such figures and traditions are to be understood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consecration of Valor (definition of Norse religion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Norse Religion as a 'Consecration of Valor' — valor is the fountain of pity, truth, and all that is great and good; by valor man becomes in some sense godlike.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The lecture treats 'Consecration of Valor' as the primary seed-grain of Norse religion: Odin's exhortation of valor made men feel divine, and from that seed grew myth, ritual, and saga. Use examples like Thor's labors and Balder's death to show how valor and robust homely vigor animate the tradition. (Original phrasing: 'That the man Odin... told his People the infinite importance of Valor... this seems to me the primary seed-grain of the Norse Religion' and later 'That Norse Religion... a rude but earnest, sternly impressive _Consecration of Valor_ (so we may define it)'.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Norse mythic character: robust simplicity, veracity, and humor
rubrics_metrics.description: The Norse poetic/moral character is marked by heartiness, homeliness, robust mirth, directness, veracity, and a 'robust homely vigor' rather than theatrical sublimity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating Norse myth or its modern retellings, prize straightforward, earthy depiction over overwrought sublimity. Examples cited: Thor 'grasps his hammer till the knuckles grow white', Balder the Sungod, and the comic-allegoric tales (e.g., Skrymir/Utgard) that combine seriousness with broad humor. The text warns that fragments (e.g., Gray) can misrepresent this tone ('Gray's fragments... will give one no notion of it').

rubrics_metrics.name: Myth as organic growth from a foundational seed
rubrics_metrics.description: Myths and religious forms grow organically from a central 'seed' (a founding idea or person) and develop into complex, interrelated branches (a 'world-tree').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The lecture stresses that a single formative figure or idea (e.g., Odin) spreads a 'shadow of his own likeness' producing sagas, allegories, and rites; the metaphor of the Banyan-tree/world-tree is used: 'the first seed is the essential thing: any branch strikes itself down into the earth, becomes a new root.' Use genealogies and cultural diffusion examples (traces in Celtic/Scottish ballads, Hamlet/Amleth) to show how mythic material is transformed across time and place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegory and play vs. prophetic/devout mythic phases
rubrics_metrics.description: Different mythic material belongs to different phases: some tales are allegoric or playful rather than prophetic/devout, and this distinction matters for interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify episodes (e.g., Thor at Utgard) as 'allegoric/half play' with symbolic meanings rather than core prophetic lore; recognize transformations where originally serious myths acquire more playful or allegorical treatments in later skaldic songs.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Hero as Prophet: second phase of hero-worship
rubrics_metrics.description: After the era when heroes were worshipped as gods, the subsequent phase regards the Great Man as God-inspired — a prophet — not a deity himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this framework to analyze receptions of major figures: distinguish divine-deification (earlier phase) from prophet/teacher status (later phase). The lecture frames this as a universal historical shift: 'The Hero is not now regarded as a God... but as one God-inspired, as a Prophet.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity as the primary characteristic of the Great Man
rubrics_metrics.description: A Great Man (hero/prophet) is first of all sincerely and deeply earnest — a kind of sincerity that is unconscious and unavoidable, not self-professed bravado.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate candidates for 'greatness' by their inner, unavoidable sincerity: 'The great Fact of Existence is great to him... he cannot help being sincere!' The lecture contrasts true sincerity with superficial 'self-conceit' and insists sincerity precedes efficacy and authenticity in leadership or prophetic claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and direct communion with the inner fact (revelation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A truly great man is 'original' — speaking at first-hand from an inner communion with reality; his utterances are akin to revelation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a leader/prophet/artist, look for evidence of first-hand vision rather than hearsay or imitation. The text describes such utterances as 'a kind of "revelation;"—what we must call such for want of some other name? ... It is from the heart of the world that he comes.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Tolerance for personal faults when inner struggle and repentance exist
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral greatness tolerates external faults if there is genuine inner remorse and an ongoing struggle toward goodness; the worst moral state is consciousness of no sin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use inner moral trajectory and repentance as criteria: the example of David ('the man according to God's own heart') is cited to argue that measurable faults do not negate moral centrality if accompanied by sincere repentance. Anti-pattern: 'the greatest of faults... to be conscious of none.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Durability and mass adherence as evidences of a religion's authenticity or conformity with nature
rubrics_metrics.description: A religion's long endurance and the large number of adherents are offered as evidence that it cannot be mere imposture or quackery; durability suggests conformity with human/natural truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The lecture argues against the idea that a successful religion was founded by a mere impostor: 'A greater number of God's creatures believe in Mahomet's word at this hour... Are we to suppose that it was a miserable piece of spiritual legerdemain?' Use longevity and widespread acceptance as heuristic indicators (not proof) of structural soundness and psychological/social fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmental and cultural shaping of religious/prophetic character
rubrics_metrics.description: Geography and social conditions (e.g., Arabian deserts, pilgrimage centers) shape the character of peoples and thereby the form and reception of religious ideas and prophets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess prophets and religious movements in context: the lecture links Arabia's 'savage inaccessible rock-mountains' and desert horizon to a people 'swift-handed, deep-hearted' and to the emergence of Mahomet. Also emphasizes Mecca's role (Black Stone, Well Zemzem, pilgrimages) as a social-economic and sacred center that enabled a shared religious culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social virtues and practices supporting religious life (hospitality, poetic contests, ritual centers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain social customs — sacred hospitality, poetic contests, tribal governance around sanctuaries like the Caabah — facilitate the formation and spread of religious movements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing origins or strength of a tradition, note communal rituals (pilgrimage), social practices (hospitality norms), and cultural institutions (poetry fairs) that bind disparate groups and create venues for diffusion (Mecca as a fair and shrine). The lecture gives specific ethnographic detail (Bedouin hospitality, Koreish governance, annual poetic contests).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mythic eschatology as expression of universal human insight (Ragnarok)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apocalyptic or eschatological myths (e.g., Ragnarok) embody a universal law of mutation: death and destruction lead to renewal — a 'phoenix fire-death' and new birth into 'the Greater and the Better'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate eschatological narratives as philosophical/psychological expressions of human insight into change and renewal. The lecture treats Ragnarok not merely as doom but as an emblem of cyclical regeneration and a 'fundamental Law of Being for a creature made of Time.'
